title: Supervision 4 essay
description: Why are ventilation and perfusion not perfectly matched in the healthy lung? Discuss how the lung limits the mismatch, and when its response can do harm.
instructions:
This is the work to hand in for Supervision 4. Write it here, the same way you’ll write your essays in the online exam.

  • Planning. Plan your essay before you start writing, on paper if you like.
  • Diagrams. You can add diagrams, just as you can in the exam. Draw one with Insert drawing (the pencil), or use Insert picture to add a picture, such as a photo of a diagram you drew on paper. Type a caption under it. Your pictures go into the Word document with your work.
  • Pasting. As in the exam, you can copy and paste within your work, but you can’t paste in text copied from anywhere else. Write everything in your own words.
  • Saving. Your work is saved in this browser as you type, so you can stop and come back to it. It stays here until you submit it.
  • When you’ve finished, go to the submission page (the ✓ tile at the bottom right), check your work and submit it. Then hand it in as described below.

questions.title: Ventilation and perfusion
questions.text:
Why are ventilation and perfusion not perfectly matched in the healthy lung? Discuss how the lung limits the mismatch, and when its response can do harm.

Write in continuous prose, with an introduction, paragraphs that each make one point, and a conclusion. Support your argument with mechanisms, evidence and numbers from the lectures.
questions.guidance:
Read this after you’ve written your essay, and use it before the supervision to look back over what you wrote. It isn’t a model essay. It sets out the ground a good answer covers.

What the title asks. Three things: the causes of mismatch in a healthy lung, the mechanisms that limit it, and when those mechanisms do harm. The best essays explain why mismatch matters at all (its effect on arterial PO2) before describing how it’s limited, and use diagrams to carry the argument.

  • The ideal and the measure. Gas exchange needs alveoli that are both ventilated and perfused. V/Q is the ratio of alveolar ventilation to blood flow: overall about 0.8 (about 4 L/min of alveolar ventilation for 5 L/min of blood). At the extremes, dead space (V/Q = ∞) and shunt (V/Q = 0).
  • Why perfusion is uneven. The pulmonary circulation is a low-pressure circuit, so the hydrostatic gradient up the upright lung matters: West’s zones. Zone 1 (PA > Pa > Pv): no flow, if it exists at all (after a haemorrhage, or with positive-pressure ventilation); zone 2 (Pa > PA > Pv): flow set by the arterial–alveolar difference; zone 3: flow set by the arterial–venous difference, highest at the base. Posture, the branching of vessels and disease change it.
  • Why ventilation is uneven. The gradient of pleural pressure (more negative at the apex) means apical alveoli are more expanded at the end of expiration, on the flat part of the compliance curve; basal alveoli are smaller and more compliant, so they expand more in each breath. Ventilation also increases down the lung, but less steeply than blood flow, so V/Q falls from about 3 at the apex to about 0.6 at the base (1 at about the third rib).
  • Why mismatch lowers arterial PO2. Blood mixes by O2 content. High-V/Q units can’t compensate for low ones, because their blood is on the flat top of the dissociation curve; CO2, with its nearly linear curve, can be compensated by extra ventilation. Hence hypoxaemia with a normal or low PCO2. Normal venous admixture (bronchial circulation, low V/Q at the bases) explains why arterial PO2 (about 95 mmHg) is lower than end-capillary PO2 (about 100 mmHg).
  • How the lung limits it. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (opposite to the systemic response; mechanism uncertain): blood is diverted from poorly ventilated alveoli (atelectasis, a foreign body) to well-ventilated ones, with little effect on pulmonary arterial pressure when the hypoxia is regional. Low PCO2 in poorly perfused units constricts their airways, shifting ventilation elsewhere. Prone positioning in ARDS evens out the distribution.
  • When it does harm. Generalised hypoxia (altitude, chronic lung disease) causes generalised vasoconstriction: pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular hypertrophy and then failure, with peripheral oedema (brisket disease in cattle, which have particularly muscular pulmonary arteries). High-altitude pulmonary oedema: high pressures, uneven constriction overperfusing some capillaries, and leak.
  • Other examples of mismatch, and how each changes V/Q: pulmonary embolism (dead space), a foreign body or mass in an airway (shunt-like), pulmonary oedema, and apical tuberculosis (high V/Q, high PO2).

What makes an essay stand out. A clear explanation of why mismatch lowers PO2 (with the dissociation curve), diagrams that the text uses, and a balanced final section: the same response that is adaptive when hypoxia is regional is harmful when it is global.
